items.question: Put the commands in order.

feedback.correct: Branch, commit, go back, merge, check, delete the label.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the one before it.

byKey.commit: You committed before making the branch, so the signal landed on main.
byKey.merge: You merged while still on carry. Switch to main first, the branch that receives.
byKey.del: You deleted carry before merging. `-d` would refuse, as its commit is not in main yet.
byKey.main: You switched to main before committing, so the edits would travel with you uncommitted.
byKey.log: Check the picture after the merge, before you remove the label.

explain.text: `switch -c` puts you on carry, so the commit moves carry. Back on main, `git merge carry` fast-forwards main. The log confirms it, and `branch -d` removes only the label.

items.prose: main has 6 commits. You make two branches at main's tip: signal-a gets 2 commits and signal-b gets 3. On main you merge signal-a, then signal-b.
items.question: How many commits does main contain at the end?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide, for each merge, whether it is a fast-forward.

byKey.two-merges: The first merge is a fast-forward: main had not moved since signal-a split off. Only the second makes a merge commit.
byKey.no-merge: The second merge cannot fast-forward. main gained signal-a's commits, so a merge commit joins signal-b.
byKey.one-branch: Both branches end up in main: 2 commits from signal-a and 3 from signal-b.

explain.text: Merging signal-a is a fast-forward, so main has 8 commits. signal-b split off before those 2, so the second merge needs a merge commit. That adds signal-b's 3 commits plus 1: 12 in all.

items.question: Complete `contains(parents, tip)`.

    todo = [tip]
    while todo:

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: a straight line, a merge commit, shared ancestors reached twice, and a 500-commit history. Each result must equal the expected set.

feedback.correct: Your function follows every parent arrow, including both of a merge's.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow every parent, and skip commits you have already seen.

explain.text: `todo.extend(parents[c])` follows every arrow, so both parents of a merge are reached. The `seen` check stops shared ancestors being visited twice. This set is what `git log` lists for a branch.

items.prose: Use `contains` to predict what `git merge other` does while you are on `current`. Return "up to date" when current already contains other, "fast-forward" when other contains current, and "merge commit" otherwise.
items.question: Complete `merge_kind(parents, current, other)`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, including merging a branch into itself and merging into a merge commit. Each result must equal the expected text exactly.

feedback.correct: Your function sorts every merge the way Git does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check "up to date" first, then "fast-forward".

explain.text: Check "up to date" first: if current already reaches other, there is nothing to bring in, even when a branch is merged into itself. If other reaches current, current is directly behind it, so Git can slide it forward. Anything else needs a merge commit.

items.title: Two signals, one reproducible main
items.prompt:
Your backtest repository's main produced `results-2026-09.md` (Sharpe 1.12). You want to test two ideas, a momentum filter and a carry signal, independently. Both will need to change `config.yaml`. Describe your plan, with the Git commands and a reason for each.
1. How you set up and work on the two ideas so that main can always reproduce the note.
2. How you bring a successful idea back. Which kind of merge do you expect for the first, and for the second?
3. What happens when both ideas changed the `lookback:` line in config.yaml, and how you resolve it.
4. A week later a merged idea turns out to have a look-ahead bug, and colleagues have pulled main. How do you undo it, and why not with reset?
items.model:
**1. One branch per idea.** From main I run `git switch -c momentum-filter`, and later, from main again, `git switch -c carry`. `-c` moves HEAD onto the new branch, so every commit moves that branch and never main. Before committing I check `git branch` for the star. main stays on the commit that wrote the note, so `git switch main` and a rerun reproduce Sharpe 1.12.

**2. Merging back.** I stand on the receiving branch: `git switch main`, then `git merge momentum-filter`. main has not moved since I branched, so this is a fast-forward. carry split off before those commits, so `git merge carry` then makes a merge commit with two parents. I check with `git log --oneline --graph` and remove the labels with `git branch -d`.

**3. The conflict.** Both branches edited `lookback:`, so the second merge stops with `CONFLICT (content)`. config.yaml shows `<<<<<<< HEAD`, main's version (now momentum's), then `=======`, then carry's, then `>>>>>>> carry`. I compare both halves with the file before the split, keep each real change, choose one lookback deliberately, and delete all three markers. Then I rerun the backtest, `git add config.yaml` and `git commit`.

**4. Undoing a shared mistake.** Colleagues have the commits, so I must not rewrite history. `git revert <commit>` adds a new commit that cancels the bug. carry came in through a merge commit, so `git revert -m 1 <merge>` cancels it whole; momentum was a fast-forward, so revert its commits one by one, newest first. `git reset --hard` would move main back, but colleagues' copies still hold those commits. Their next merge would bring the bug back and the histories would disagree.

rubric.text: Uses one branch per idea, made with `git switch -c` (not `git branch` alone), so main never moves while experimenting
Explains that main stays on the commit that produced the note, so switching back reproduces it
Merges by switching to main first and naming the idea branch
Predicts a fast-forward for the first merge and a merge commit with two parents for the second, with the reason
Resolves the conflict: reads the markers, compares with the old file and deletes every marker. Then runs `git add` and `git commit`
Undoes the shared mistake with `git revert`, and explains why reset is unsafe once others have the commits
